newsitem.title: BELGIUM: JOBS-European data a potential source of confusion.
newsitem.headline: JOBS-European data a potential source of confusion.

text.p: Is Germany's unemployment rate higher or lower than Sweden's? Does Finland have a jobless rate of 15 percent or closer to 20 percent?
Was Belgium's unemployment rate 9.5 percent in December, well below the European Union average, or as high as 13.6 percent?
All of these conclusions, however contradictory, find support in the complex world of labour market statistics. It all depends on how you define "unemployed" -- and the answer varies.
That can make direct comparisons risky.
"The message should be: if you compare across countries use a measure that is comparable," said an official at Eurostat, the EU's statistics office.

Some of the EU's 15 countries prefer to measure unemployment by conducting surveys asking people whether they are unemployed and actively seeking work, while others use the number of registered unemployed claiming jobless benefits.
There are even those, like Finland, that issue two sets of figures, showing at times widely different jobless rates.
"To a certain extent you could say that some countries somewhat overestimate or underestimate employment in comparison with other member states," the Eurostat official said.
The data based on registered unemployed is quicker and cheaper to put together and is also more exhaustive as it is used administratively for paying employment benefits.

The Eurostat figures, and those issued by national statistics bureaus, are based on surveys in which a sample of people are polled and registered as being with or without work depending on their replies.

To take one example of potentially confusing data: the national unemployment figures for December issued by Statistics Sweden and Germany's Federal Labour Office showed Sweden in a much better position, with a jobless rate of 8.7 percent compared with Germany's 10.8 percent.
However, according to Eurostat, which puts out more harmonised and comparable data, Sweden had a higher jobless rate of 10.6 to Germany's 9.3 percent. EUROSTAT ISSUES COMPARABLE JOBLESS FIGURES

Eurostat, which issues monthly unemployment figures for the EU and its member states, bases its calculations on the recommendation of the International Labour Office (ILO), a Geneva-based specialised agency of the United Nations.
The Eurostat official said figures provided by his body or by the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) should be used in international comparisons.

"There you have more guarantees that the categories included or excluded from unemployment are the same," he said. The United States and Japan base their calculations on the ILO's method, making their figures comparable with those of Eurostat.

For Eurostat, the unemployed are those who are at least 15 years old and fulfill three conditions: they are without work, are available to start work within the next two weeks and have actively sought a job at some point during the previous four weeks.
This definition may exclude, for example, pregnant women as they may be unable to start working at such short notice, even if they are looking for a job.
However, even if a country follows the ILO's recommendation it may arrive at a different figure than Eurostat by excluding certain groups from its calculations.
"The mathematical method may not be different, but people who fit into it may be different," said an ILO official.

For example, Sweden's December jobless rate was reported differently by Statistics Sweden and Eurostat because Sweden does not include some 100,000 students, even if they say they are unemployed and want work. According to the ILO, these students are unemployed.

But the more usual reason for differences between Eurostat's figures and those issued nationally is that some countries -- for example, Germany and Belgium -- calculate their monthly jobless rates based on the number of registered unemployed.
That often produces worse jobless figures than the ones published by Eurostat.

"As soon as you start to talk about registered unemployment there is one major risk -- the registered unemployed may be people who have a job," the Eurostat official said, referring to possible part-time jobs.
According to one EU official, the number of persons registered as unemployed in Germany is significantly higher than the "real number of ILO-unemployed."

That helps explain why Germany's Federal Labour Office reported a 10.8 percent jobless rate for December while Eurostat reported a rate of 9.3 percent. Furthermore, the labour office's rate, unlike that of Eurostat, is not seasonally adjusted. WAS BELGIUM'S JOBLESS RATE 9.5 OR 13.6 % IN DECEMBER?
Belgium's Employment Ministry reported a December jobless rate of 13.6 percent, based on the number of registered unemployed, while Eurostat said it was 9.5 percent.
Listing registered unemployment benefit claimants, Denmark's national statistics office reported a December jobless rate of 8.1 percent. Eurostat said it was 5.5 percent.
"It can be a big difference, and depending on population groups, age groups, it can even increase," the ILO official said.

Finland is one of a few EU countries which publish two sets of monthly jobless figures, one by Statistics Finland (SF) based on the ILO's recommendation and one by the Labour Ministry based on the number of registered job seekers.
While SF reported that 15.5 percent of the workforce was unemployed in December, the ministry put the rate at 19 percent.
The EU official, comparing unemployment with illness, said that calculations based on the ILO's recommendation measured those who were ill.
In contrast, the "registered unemployed" covers all those who went to the doctor -- even if they would not be considered unemployed by the ILO, he said.
To avoid confusion, the ILO official stressed the importance of always making clear which calculation method was used.
